title: Segregated eating on the road and in Birmingham
summary: He describes taking food out, back-door service, soul food in Birmingham and the Palm Beach Hotel.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I see. What about from people stopping you, and racial incidents, and that sort of thing? When Oliver was traveling, did he ever encounter that? Did your band ever encounter any of those problems?
Well, I had a little (?) in Wichita, Kansas.

I could feel(?) it(?), and I could see certain places we could eat... In a lot of them places down South, you couldn't eat. You'd have to go in... You'd take it out. They'd wrap it up as it was, and you'd take it out, you
know. Sometimes they'd let you eat in some places, but you had to go in the back door.
You had to go in the back door; the side door, they called it. When you'd come in, they'd look right straight in front of you, you know. You'd see you're not wanted in there, you know.

Before we'd get a chance to tell the man what we wanted to eat, he'd tell us "The place is not open; come back later." But you had to come around the back door. I didn't never go back there, though, or nothin'... I used to go to the grocery store and get me a couple of rolls and some cheese, liverwurst, stuff like that, you know. A lot of food like that. You can't eat very much on it, because it's kind of hard to get those places ...(? )...(? )... When you eat different places...

Now, when I was in Birmingham, Alabama, they had one place I'd eat. That was... They had Soul...what they call Soul Food. Black beans, rice, and collard greens, roast beef, pork chops -- all that kind of food, you know. Cornbread... That was three dollars a week, two meals a day. Of course, I stayed at the hotel, paying thirty-five dollars a week for the hotel. The Palm Beach Hotel on Fourteenth
Street and Fourth Avenue, right across the street from the theatre -- I was at the Prolie Theatre then.
